scenes.narration: Four bugs chase each other around a square. Each always aims at the next bug, and all move at the same constant speed. Their paths curl inward. How far does each bug travel before they meet? The starting square is four meters wide. The answer is exactly four meters, even though the path is a spiral. Here is the trick: ignore the whole spiral for a moment. Watch just one bug and its target. By symmetry, the four bugs keep forming a smaller, turning square. The chasing bug moves directly along one side toward its target. The target moves along the next side, at a right angle. At that instant, its motion contributes nothing along the gap between them. Only the chaser closes that gap. If the speed is one meter per second, the gap shrinks by one meter per second. Watch the remaining gap and the traveled-distance bar together. One loses exactly what the other gains. We started with a four-meter gap, so it takes four seconds to vanish. At one meter per second, each bug travels four meters. The spiral can wind ever more tightly near the center without requiring extra distance beyond that total. This drawing stops just before the exact meeting point. Double the starting square, keeping the speed the same. The chase takes twice as long, and each path is twice as long. A complicated curve became simple when we measured the right gap.
